items.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: All the guys that I came up playing with... Pat Martino, same kind of thing.

ctx.x: I couldn’t agree more. What experiences have you had perhaps with Charles Earland or some of the other fellows that you were a sideman with that impacted your eventual role as a leader. Did you learn stuff from those guys musically and otherwise that helped you out?

Well I’ve been lucky. All the guys that I came up playing with, one of the things they shared is they play music like it’s the last time they’ll ever play. It’s almost like somebody said, “This is the last song you’re ever going to play, you better have fun.” They give everything they have at all times. I guess it’s just that they respect — I mean they’re not thinking about it but if you had to give a reason why are they playing it, they just respect and love the music so much. They would never give less than a…

percent. I remember playing with Charles Earland in this huge room in Rochester, it was Thanksgiving 1990. Was is ’90 or ’91? Maybe it was ’91. And there were maybe four people in this cavernous room. And he played like a two hour set and almost blew the organ up and was sweating all over the place. What’s he doing? Why is he doing this? Can’t we just go home? But this stuff started to rub off on me. Playing with Harold? I mean if you don’t bring your A game and really step up, he going over, it’s like a tsunami.…
